description: Vocal and physical choices that capture the inequality and intimacy between the two leads.
content_html:
The Challenge of Playing Across a Power Gap

Performing the central relationship in Noughts and Crosses asks two actors to hold a seemingly contradictory truth at the same time: Sephy and Callum are drawn to each other with the intensity of a long childhood friendship and a growing romantic attachment, yet they inhabit radically different positions in the society the play depicts. Sephy is the daughter of a senior Cross politician; Callum is the son of her family’s former nought servant. Every moment they share is charged with the inequality of their social positions, even when neither character wants to acknowledge it.

The performing challenge is to make this tension visible in the body and voice without oversimplifying it. An actor who plays Callum as simply angry, or one who plays Sephy as simply naive, misses the play’s complexity. The best performances find the specific moment when each character’s awareness of the social gap flickers into view — and then is suppressed.

Key Fact

In performance questions, “I would act angrily” scores in the Emerging band. A Mastering-level answer names the specific vocal quality (reduced volume and pace, lowering pitch at the end of a phrase to signal resignation) AND the specific physical choice (stillness, weight held back over the rear foot rather than the forward foot, minimal eye contact redirected to a fixed neutral point rather than Sephy’s face).

Proxemics: Distance as Drama

Proxemics — the meaningful use of physical distance between performers — is central to almost every scene Sephy and Callum share. When they were children on the beach, the open distance between them communicated freedom; as the play progresses, their closeness becomes simultaneously more charged and more impossible. A director might choose to stage confrontation scenes so that the two performers are physically close but turned slightly away from each other, bodies angled at forty-five degrees — close enough to touch but blocked from full face-to-face contact. This physical arrangement communicates the emotional truth of the scene in a way that no amount of dialogue analysis can match.

In contrast, the moments of brief, genuine connection — the hostage scene where they are isolated together, or the quiet private exchanges in the Hadley garden — might use maximum physical proximity, the performers turning to face each other fully, with all the vulnerability that entails. The shift from angled-away to fully facing is a tiny physical action that carries enormous theatrical weight.

Sephy is written as someone whose social privilege is so deeply embedded that she does not fully see it — at least initially. A performer playing Sephy in scenes of early conflict with Callum might make the following specific choices:

Pace: slightly faster than natural speech in moments of enthusiasm, slowing abruptly when she realises she has said something that marks her privilege — the hesitation itself becomes a performance of growing awareness.

Pitch: higher registers for warmth and excitement; a dropping of pitch and volume when the subject turns to Callum’s family’s situation — a physical sign of social discomfort she cannot articulate.

Gesture: open, expansive hand gestures when speaking about her own world; hands pulled in, perhaps clasped or held at the waist, when acknowledging what Callum faces. The body language of privilege retreating from its own implications.

Callum inhabits every Cross space as someone acutely aware of being watched and assessed. A performer playing Callum in the school scene or the Hadley home might make these specific physical choices:

Posture: upright and controlled, shoulders slightly drawn back — not relaxed, but effortful. The tension of someone who has decided to present a composed surface. This differs from natural relaxation; the audience should see the work it takes to hold this posture.

Eye contact: deliberately calibrated — sustained direct eye contact with Sephy in private scenes to signal genuine connection; redirected or lowered in scenes with authority figures, the physical embodiment of learned survival in a hostile environment.

Movement through space: in Cross spaces, Callum might move with economical, contained steps, avoiding large gestures or sweeping arm movements — the physical signature of someone who has learned not to take up too much space. This can be made very specific: when standing upstage while Cross characters occupy downstage positions, his physical retreat has a visual grammar the audience reads as social exclusion.

Stillness as Meaning

In the confrontation scenes and the courtroom moment, stillness becomes a primary performance tool. A performer who moves too much during an interrogation or courtroom scene dissipates the tension; the character who is most still is often the one who communicates the most control — or the most fear of losing it. A performer playing Callum under interrogation might make the choice to be almost entirely physically still, weight settled, hands visible and open on the knees or chair arms, only the small involuntary movements — a swallow, a barely perceptible tightening around the eyes — betraying the interior state.

This is what the spec means by subtext in performance: the gap between what is shown and what is felt. A performer communicates subtext not by performing the feeling openly but by performing the effort of containing it. The more specific the physical detail of that containment — where the hands are, whether the breath is held or controlled — the more clearly the subtext registers with the audience.

Key Fact

The difference between tableau and mere stillness is intentionality: a tableau is chosen and composed, every performer’s position part of a collective image. In confrontation scenes or in the final letter sequence, a director might freeze the scene into a deliberate tableau — giving the audience a sustained visual image of the relationship’s final state before the narrative resolves it.
exam_tip_html:
The most frequent error in the 8-mark Interpret as Performer question is describing what the character is feeling rather than translating that feeling into specific vocal and physical choices. The command is ‘how would you interpret’ — not ‘what is the character feeling’. Your answer must do three things: name the feeling or intention, name the specific vocal choice that communicates it (with detail: not just ‘slowly’ but ‘deliberate reduction in pace across the final phrase, with a pause before the last word’), and name the specific physical choice (not just ‘looks down’ but ‘redirects gaze downstage left to a fixed neutral point, breaking eye contact with the other performer for the first time in the scene’). Both vocal and physical must appear — a mark scheme that requires both will not award Mastering for one alone.

For the 20-mark extended response, anchor every choice to a named moment of the play. Vague references to ‘scenes where they disagree’ score in the Developing band. Named moments — the school confrontation, the interrogation scene, the hostage scene, the final letter — anchor your staging decisions in specifics the examiner can recognise and reward.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Performing the central relationship requires holding intimacy and inequality in tension simultaneously; specific proxemic choices — forty-five-degree body angles, the shift from avoidance to full face-to-face — communicate this tension more precisely than any amount of general ‘acting angrily’.
  • Subtext in performance is communicated through the effort of containment, not through the open expression of feeling; stillness, controlled breath, calibrated eye contact and economical movement are the specific tools that make interior states visible without stating them.
  • In exam answers, always name both a vocal choice (pace, pitch, volume, pause, tone) and a physical choice (posture, gesture, eye contact, movement pattern, position on stage) for the named moment — and always explain what the choice communicates to the audience, not just to the character.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to show Sephy's social discomfort in a scene with Callum.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one named vocal skill with brief justification: e.g. slowing pace when she recognises her privilege / dropping pitch and volume / pausing before key words / hesitation / quiet delivery.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'subtext' in acting and performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that subtext is what is implied or felt beneath the surface of the dialogue; 1 mark for explaining that a performer communicates subtext not by expressing the feeling openly but by performing the effort of containing or concealing it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of proxemics in a scene between Sephy and Callum. In your answer, refer to a specific scene from the play and describe a specific staging choice, explaining what it communicates to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of proxemics as the use of physical distance and orientation between performers (1), description of a specific proxemic choice for a named scene (e.g. the two performers positioned close but body-angled away from each other in a confrontation scene) (1), explanation of what that choice communicates about the power gap or emotional tension between the characters (1), explanation of the effect this creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Callum in the interrogation scene, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate his attempt to maintain composure under pressure. Refer to specific choices and name the effect you want them to have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): both vocal and physical choices named and specific; vocal: e.g. controlled, measured pace with deliberate pauses before responses, lowered pitch, reduced volume to signal control; physical: e.g. almost entirely still, weight settled, hands open and visible, only involuntary micro-movements betraying interior state, sustained but carefully chosen eye contact with the interrogator; each choice linked to the character's intention (to survive without giving anything away) and to the audience's experience (they feel the effort of containment, making the subtext palpable); named moment referenced.
Secure (5-6): both vocal and physical present; generally specific; at least one named moment; effect on audience identified.
Developing (3-4): relevant ideas but one dimension only (vocal or physical), or generic descriptors ('acts calmly', 'moves carefully'); effect implied.
Emerging (1-2): basic description of how the character feels with little or no translation into specific performance choices.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's and director's intentions in showing the relationship between Sephy and Callum through contrasting scenes of intimacy and confrontation. What do you think they want the audience to understand about love and inequality by placing these scenes alongside each other?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): sustained analysis of intentional juxtaposition of intimacy and confrontation; argues that placing love and inequality in the same relationship forces the audience to confront the personal cost of systemic racism; at least two named scenes discussed; specific staging, vocal and physical implications explored; considers both Blackman's original intent and Cooke's adaptation choices; substantiated judgement about cumulative audience response.
Secure (7-9): clear analysis with some reference to intention; at least one named scene; generally accurate effect identified; good understanding of the relationship's central tension.
Developing (4-6): relevant but mostly descriptive; retells what happens in scenes rather than analysing intention; limited named moments.
Emerging (1-3): basic identification of the relationship with little or no analysis of intention.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how you would stage the beach scene (in which Sephy and Callum are together as young people, before the politics intensify) and a later confrontation scene of your choice. For each scene, describe the performers' positioning and physical choices, the lighting design and any sound or set elements that communicate the change in their relationship. Explain what effect you want these staging choices to have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): detailed staging vision for both scenes; beach scene: open proxemics, warm lighting, spacious stage, performers' physical freedom and open body language; later confrontation: reduced proxemics or angled-away positioning, colder lighting state, physical containment and tension; at least one specific lighting element per scene (named gel colour or effect, lantern type); at least one sound or set element per scene; every choice anchored to named moment and explained in terms of audience effect; coherent directorial vision that shows awareness of the journey from openness to loss.
Secure (12-16): both scenes addressed; most design areas covered; at least one specific choice per area; named moments referenced; some justification.
Developing (7-11): relevant ideas but generic terminology; limited specificity; effects implied; may only address one scene in detail.
Emerging (1-6): basic staging ideas with little technical vocabulary; plot retelling may intrude.

options: The literal meaning of the dialogue spoken by a character
What a character thinks or feels but does not say openly, communicated through performance choices
The stage directions written by the playwright
The character's backstory as described in the programme

knowledge_checks.q: In exam answers about performer choices, which response would score in the Mastering band?
options: I would use a loud voice
I would move slowly to show sadness
I would reduce pace across the final phrase, pausing before the last word, and redirect gaze to a fixed neutral point, breaking eye contact for the first time in the scene

knowledge_checks.q: Proxemics refers to the meaningful use of physical _____ between performers on stage.
A fixed, held position in which performers freeze to create a visual image is called a _____.
Match each performance concept to its correct definition:
right: What a character feels but does not say openly, communicated through physical and vocal containment
The use of distance and orientation between performers to communicate status and emotion
A frozen, composed visual image created by performers to communicate meaning

flashcard_questions.a: What a character feels but does not say openly, communicated by the performer containing rather than expressing the emotion.
The physical relationship between performers on stage, including distance and orientation, used to communicate status and emotion.
A fixed, held stage image in which performers freeze, every position contributing to a composed visual meaning.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two vocal skills a performer might use to communicate contained emotion.
flashcard_questions.a: Reduced pace and controlled, lower pitch to signal effort of suppression.
Towards the front of the stage, closest to the audience.
Towards the back of the stage, furthest from the audience.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a performer show subtext rather than simply acting the emotion?
flashcard_questions.a: By performing the effort of containing or concealing the feeling through precise physical and vocal choices.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a forty-five-degree body angle between two performers communicate?
flashcard_questions.a: Physical proximity without full openness — closeness combined with emotional guardedness or social constraint.

flashcard_questions.q: Who are the two central characters in Noughts and Crosses?
What social positions do Sephy and Callum occupy in the world of the play?
flashcard_questions.a: Sephy is the daughter of a senior Cross politician; Callum is the son of the family's former nought servant.
A gesture or physical attitude that captures a character's social relationship and attitude in a single condensed image.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one physical choice a performer playing Callum in a Cross space might make to show his learned self-containment.
flashcard_questions.a: Economical, contained movement — small steps, no large gestures, upright controlled posture achieved through effort.

glossary_terms.definition: The physical relationship between performers on stage, including distance and orientation, used to communicate status, emotion and relationship.
The quality beneath the surface of dialogue — what a character thinks or feels but does not say openly, communicated through performance choices.
A fixed, held position in which performers freeze to create a composed visual image that communicates meaning.
A Brechtian concept describing a gesture or physical attitude that captures a character's social relationship in a single condensed image.
Towards the back of the stage, furthest from the audience.
Towards the front of the stage, closest to the audience.
When one performer plays more than one character in the same production, often used to reflect social types rather than individuals.
